title: Stop Pretending Novices Are Little Experts
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: Drawing on cognitive science and expertise research, this article challenges the foundational assumption of many student-centred instructional models: that novices can learn effectively by performing expert-level tasks. The author argues that experts and novices do not think in the same way, and that placing students in roles requiring expert cognition — teaching peers, evaluating sources, facilitating discussion, generating hypotheses — imposes crushing cognitive load precisely when students lack the knowledge structures needed to manage it. The jigsaw strategy receives extended scrutiny as a case study: students asked to 'become experts' in a few minutes and then teach peers are not experts at all, and the dual demand of learning-while-teaching overwhelms working memory. The article does not oppose collaboration or discussion but insists that these activities must come after students have acquired enough knowledge to participate meaningfully. The piece calls for instructional design that sequences explicit guidance first and student-directed activity second, in proportion to where students actually are on the novice-to-expert continuum.
points: Expertise is not a quantity of facts but a qualitatively different cognitive architecture. Experts recognize patterns, anticipate misconceptions, and think in well-organised schemas that free working memory — none of which novices possess simply by being placed in expert-like roles.

The jigsaw strategy's fatal assumption is that a student who has spent fifteen minutes with new material is capable of expert-level teaching: determining what matters most, organizing ideas coherently, monitoring peer understanding, and correcting misconceptions — all simultaneously.

Cognitive load theory explains why student-centred lessons frequently fail: working memory is severely limited, and asking novices to learn content while simultaneously performing teaching tasks overwhelms the system, producing the appearance of engagement without actual learning.

Visible activity in a classroom is not evidence of learning. Collaborative noise, movement, and participation can coexist with near-zero knowledge retention if the cognitive demands of the task exceed what the learner can manage.

Sophisticated thinking — critical reasoning, synthesis, evaluation, creative problem-solving — is not a skill that develops independently of content knowledge; it emerges from knowledge. Instructional designs that invert this sequence produce neither the knowledge nor the thinking.
quotes: One of the most robust findings to emerge from cognitive science is that experts and novices do not think in the same way. This difference is not simply a matter of experts knowing more facts or possessing greater intelligence. Rather, experts have developed extensive, well-organized networks of domain-specific knowledge that fundamentally alter how they process information, solve problems, and make decisions.

Many of the most celebrated student-centered approaches seem to rest on assumptions that are difficult to reconcile with what cognitive science tells us about how expertise develops. While these approaches are often praised for increasing activity, engagement, collaboration, and student ownership, they frequently place students in situations that require forms of thinking that are characteristic of experts rather than novices.

The student in a jigsaw activity is not an expert. The student is a novice who has had a brief encounter with new information. Yet the structure of the activity assumes that this novice is capable of performing tasks that are normally associated with expertise. The result is that students often find themselves struggling not only to learn the material but also to teach it simultaneously.

Advocates of student-centered learning often point to the level of activity taking place during these lessons as evidence of their effectiveness. Students are talking. Students are moving. Students are collaborating. The classroom appears intellectually vibrant. Yet visible activity is not the same thing as learning.

Many student-centered instructional approaches invert this relationship. Rather than helping students acquire the knowledge that makes expert thinking possible, they often assume that placing students in expert-like roles will somehow produce expert-like knowledge and thinking. Cognitive science suggests the opposite.

The ability to think critically, solve problems, and reason effectively is heavily dependent upon what one already knows. Instructional designs that ignore this sequence deprive students of both the knowledge and the thinking the lesson was meant to produce.
